study_identification_part.si4_title: Closing the life-cycle of normative modeling using federated hierarchical Bayesian regression

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To introduce a federated probabilistic framework using hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) to complete the life-cycle of normative modeling, addressing medical data privacy issues and difficulties in dealing with nuisance variation such as site-effects in multi-center neuroimaging datasets.

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Euler number thresholding (scan-site median-centered absolute Euler number > 25) with 1566 subjects (4%) excluded; manual examination of threshold; Euler number computed as part of FreeSurfer recon-all pipeline
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: We have excluded participants with missing demographic (age/sex) information and those with poor quality imaging data. We excluded 1566 (4%) subjects due to low-quality images. Subjects were excluded if their scan-site median-centered absolute Euler number was higher than 25. The Euler numbers are computed as a part of standard recon-all Freesurfer [54] pipeline. The exclusion of outliers based on Euler numbers has been shown to be a reliable quality control strategy in large neuroimaging cohorts [55, 56]. Median centering is necessary because the Euler number is scaled differently for different datasets. The threshold of 25 was determined empirically by manually examining the excluded scans.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) with scanner as random/group-effect; site-specific location (fμ) and scale (fσ) parameters estimated; weakly-informative hyperpriors over parameters (μθμ, μθσ ~ N(0, 10³); log(σθμ), log(σθσ) ~ N(0, 2.5)); compared against naive pooling, fixed-effect pooling, ComBat harmonization, and no-pooling; validation via SVM classification of z-scores showing site-effect removal (balanced accuracy drop from 0.90 to ~0.53)
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: we propose a partial pooling approach based on hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) as a possible solution for completing the life-cycle of normative modeling... In HBR, the structural dependencies between parameters are incorporated in the modeling process by coupling them via a shared prior distribution over parameters. To adopt HBR for multi-site normative modeling, we assume θμi and θσi in Eq 4 (that govern the data generating process for each batch yi) are coming exchangeably from the same prior distribution, i.e., ∀i; θμi ~ N(μθμ, σ²θμ) and θσi ~ N(μθσ, σ²θσ)... We use a wide Gaussian distribution as a weakly-informative hyperprior over parameters of the priors (μθμ, μθσ ~ N(0, 10³) and log(σθμ), log(σθσ) ~ N(0, 2.5))... The z-statistics are computed using different modeling approaches including naive pooling (NV-POOLING), fixed-effect pooling (FE-POOLING), pooling after ComBat harmonization (CMB-POOLING) and HBR. The results show that the site-effects are to high degree not present in the z-statistics in FE-POOLING, CMB-POOLING, and HBR.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Region-wise area under the ROC curve (AUC) to evaluate predictive power of abnormal probability indices for each diagnosis. Statistical significance tested via permutation tests (1000 repetitions) with FDR correction across 148 regions. Only significant and stable areas (passing FDR in 9+ out of 10 experimental runs) reported. Performance comparisons show deviations are distinctive for dementia (temporal/occipital lobes, AUC 0.64-0.68), schizophrenia (frontal lobe, AUC 0.58-0.61), and early psychosis (right middle temporal gyrus, AUC 0.59).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: HBR successfully derives accurate normative ranges on multi-site data, enables federated learning and model adaptation to local datasets with few-shot learning capabilities, and detects significant deviations in dementia (temporal/occipital regions), schizophrenia (frontal lobe), and early psychosis (temporal regions) consistent with known pathology.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) approach showed superior performance compared to naive pooling, fixed-effect pooling, ComBat harmonization, and no-pooling methods in deriving normative ranges of cortical thickness. The HBR and fixed-effect models performed equivalently well, but HBR offers advantages in federated learning scenarios. Site-effects were successfully removed from z-statistics, with balanced classification accuracy dropping from 0.90 (naive pooling) to ~0.53 (near chance) for HBR, ComBat, and fixed-effect approaches. The federated model extension strategy showed very close performance to centralized training (R² = 0.98 for correlation, 0.97 for SMSE, 0.95 for MSLL). Model adaptation with informative priors outperformed no-pooling approaches on clinical datasets. In anomaly detection, dementia patients showed significant deviations in bilateral occipitotemporal (fusiform) gyrus (AUC = 0.68 and 0.64), right middle temporal gyrus (AUC = 0.65), right superior/transverse occipital sulcus (AUC = 0.65), and right middle occipital gyrus (AUC = 0.65). Schizophrenia patients showed distinctive deviations in frontal regions including right orbital inferior frontal gyrus (AUC = 0.61), right medial orbital sulcus (AUC = 0.60), left superior frontal gyrus (AUC = 0.58), and left middle frontal sulcus (AUC = 0.58). Early psychosis showed significant deviations only in right middle temporal gyrus (AUC = 0.59). The HBR model demonstrated few-shot learning capabilities, providing reasonable normative range estimates even with 0-1 training samples at some sites, leveraging informative priors from the reference model.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Gaussian likelihood assumption may not be appropriate for skewed or bounded phenotypes; models estimated separately for each brain region without accounting for inter-regional correlations, leaving some multivariate site-effects; quality control relies on Euler number which, while validated, may not be bullet-proof; linear models used for most experiments may not capture non-linear effects present in some neuroimaging measures; clinical populations include only mild dementia cases (OASIS3), limiting comparability to studies with more advanced forms
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The current implementation of HBR employs a Gaussian likelihood function, hence, assumes a Gaussian distribution for residuals. If this is not the case, the estimated centiles and z-scores might not be well-calibrated... Another limitation is that models are estimated separately for each brain region without accounting for correlations between brain regions... in all benchmarked models, the harmonization and modeling are performed separately for each brain region without accounting for correlations between brain regions. Hence, only univariate site-effects are removed, and still, some multivariate site-effect might be present in data... While manual QC on massive datasets is costly and not practical, there is still no bullet-proof automatic QC method available in the field... Note that the patients with dementia were derived from the OASIS3 dataset, which contains only mild cases. Therefore, the accuracies reported are not directly comparable with studies derived from patients with more advanced forms of dementia.
caa10_key_limitations.location: Kia2022.pdf.md: Discussion / Limitations and future directions, L399-406; Results / The deviations are distinctive, L318-319

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study introduces a federated learning framework enabling model development on decentralized data without data sharing, addressing privacy concerns. Transfer learning via informative priors enables adaptation to small local datasets (few-shot learning). The approach is modular and can accommodate non-linear effects, heteroscedastic noise, and non-Gaussian distributions. Comparison with ComBat shows HBR preserves unknown biological variance correlated with site-effects, unlike harmonization. The method is implemented in PCNtoolkit v0.18 using PyMC3 with NUTS sampler and non-centered parameterizations for computational efficiency.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This paper presents a methodological framework rather than a traditional clinical neuroimaging study. The main contribution is the hierarchical Bayesian regression approach for federated normative modeling. The study includes 16 datasets with 37126 scans from 79 scanners, making it one of the largest normative modeling studies. The federated learning approach allows model extension (adding datasets sequentially) and model adaptation (transferring to new sites) without sharing raw data. The study demonstrates that HBR is equivalent to fixed-effect pooling in performance but offers practical advantages for decentralized scenarios. Simulation studies in supplementary materials illustrate theoretical limitations of ComBat harmonization when hidden factors correlate with site-effects and covariates. The weakly-informative hyperpriors (μ ~ N(0, 10³); log(σ) ~ N(0, 2.5)) were chosen to balance flexibility and computational efficiency. Clinical validation focused on cortical thickness as this measure shows strong site-effects and well-studied aging effects. The study excluded 1566 subjects (4%) based on Euler number QC. FreeSurfer versions 5.3 and 6.0 were both used across different datasets.
